quests.question: The feedback from my colleagues ___ I received after the presentation was surprisingly positive.
quests.hint: 'From my colleagues' just tells you the source - check what 'I' actually received.
quests.explanation: 'I received' the feedback, not the colleagues themselves - this is an object relative clause modifying 'the feedback,' so the pronoun can be dropped entirely.

quests.question: The offer from the other company ___ ultimately convinced her to switch jobs.
quests.hint: 'From the other company' just tells you the source - check what actually did the convincing.
quests.explanation: 'The offer' - not 'the company' - is what convinced her, so this is a subject relative clause; the pronoun cannot be dropped, and 'which' is correct since an offer is a thing.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: The concerns ___ residents raised at the town hall meeting went unresolved for months.
quests.hint: 'Residents' already has a job in this clause - 'raised.' What does that leave for the concerns, and does the pronoun even need to stay?
quests.explanation: 'Residents' is the subject of 'raised,' so 'the concerns' is the object being raised; since concerns are things, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.

quests.question: The professor who wrote the textbook we used all semester later won a national teaching award. What does the omitted clause 'we used all semester' describe?
quests.hint: Work backward - what did 'we' actually use all semester?
quests.explanation: 'We used' the textbook, not the professor or the award, so 'the textbook' is the antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.

quests.question: The engineer ___ designed the bridge we cross every day used to work for the city.
quests.hint: Check the first gap: does 'designed' already have a subject elsewhere in the sentence?
quests.explanation: 'Designed' has no other subject, so 'the engineer' must supply it - the pronoun cannot be dropped here, and 'who' is correct since the engineer is a person.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which of the sentences shown is grammatically correct?
quests.hint: Check both clauses separately: one needs its pronoun to stay, and the other has correctly dropped it.
quests.explanation: 'Who assigned the essay' correctly keeps 'who' since it's a subject relative clause about a person; 'we submitted yesterday' correctly drops its pronoun since it's an object relative clause about a thing.
options: The teacher assigned the essay who we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
The teacher who assigned the essay we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
The teacher which assigned the essay we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
The teacher who assigned the essay whom we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
quests.correctAnswer: The teacher who assigned the essay we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which of these sentences is grammatically correct?
quests.hint: Not every sentence needs a relative pronoun - check whether this sentence is even describing one noun with extra information about it.
quests.explanation: This is a simple sentence with no relative clause at all - there's no second noun being described by a clause, so no relative pronoun belongs here. Inserting 'that,' 'which,' or 'who' breaks the sentence.
options: I bought a new phone yesterday.
I bought that a new phone yesterday.
I bought which a new phone yesterday.
I bought who a new phone yesterday.
quests.correctAnswer: I bought a new phone yesterday.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly completes this idea, if any relative pronoun is even needed: 'She adopted a rescue dog last spring'?
quests.hint: Ask yourself: is there a second noun anywhere in this sentence that needs its own describing clause?
quests.explanation: This sentence simply states what she did - there's no additional noun being described by a clause, so no relative pronoun is needed anywhere in the sentence.
options: She adopted a rescue dog that last spring.
She adopted that a rescue dog last spring.
She adopted a rescue dog last spring.
She that adopted a rescue dog last spring.
quests.correctAnswer: She adopted a rescue dog last spring.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly completes this idea: 'She adopted a rescue dog. The dog had been abandoned twice before.'?
quests.hint: This time, there genuinely IS a second idea describing the dog - check where the connecting word belongs and whether it can be dropped.
quests.explanation: Unlike the previous example, this sentence needs a relative clause to add the fact that the dog had been abandoned; since 'had been abandoned' has no other subject, the pronoun 'that' must stay.
options: She adopted a rescue dog had been abandoned twice before.
She adopted a rescue dog last spring.
She adopted a rescue dog that had been abandoned twice before.
She that adopted a rescue dog had been abandoned twice before.
quests.correctAnswer: She adopted a rescue dog that had been abandoned twice before.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which one of these sentences is correctly written?
quests.hint: Check whether this sentence has a second noun anywhere that needs extra description via a clause.
quests.explanation: This is a complete, simple sentence describing what the team did - there's no relative clause needed here at all.
options: The team finished the project ahead of schedule.
The team finished which the project ahead of schedule.
The team that finished the project ahead of schedule.
The team finished the project that ahead of schedule.
quests.correctAnswer: The team finished the project ahead of schedule.

quests.question: Which version here is grammatically correct?
quests.hint: This is a simple statement about what the results did - check whether any noun here truly needs an extra describing clause.
quests.explanation: 'The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting' is already a complete, correct sentence; inserting 'that' or 'which' either creates a sentence fragment or unnecessarily complicates a sentence that needs no relative clause.
options: The results of the survey that surprised everyone at the meeting.
The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting.
The results that of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting.
The results of the survey which surprised everyone at the meeting occurred.
quests.correctAnswer: The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting.

quests.question: The results of the survey ___ our team conducted last quarter surprised everyone at the meeting.
quests.hint: 'Our team' already has a job in this clause - 'conducted.' What does that leave for the results, and does the pronoun even need to stay?
quests.explanation: 'Our team' is the subject of 'conducted,' so 'the results' is the object being conducted upon; since results are things, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely: 'the results our team conducted.'

quests.question: Which version fits a formal business report?
quests.hint: Formal reports generally spell out every grammatical element rather than relying on casual shortcuts.
quests.explanation: 'That we selected' is the fully written, formal version appropriate for a business report; the pronoun is retained rather than dropped.
options: The vendor we selected offers better pricing.
The vendor selected offers better pricing.
The vendor which selected offers better pricing.
The vendor that we selected offers better pricing.
quests.correctAnswer: The vendor that we selected offers better pricing.

quests.question: Which version would you most likely text a friend?
quests.hint: Texts tend to be short and casual - which option drops the unnecessary connecting word?
quests.explanation: 'The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!' is the shortest, most natural phrasing for a casual text, dropping the object relative pronoun entirely.
options: The apartment that we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!
The apartment which we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!
The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!
The apartment whom we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!
quests.correctAnswer: The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!

quests.question: Whether you're texting a friend or writing a formal report, which version of this sentence is always correct?
quests.hint: Unlike object relative clauses, this type of clause never allows the pronoun to be dropped - not even informally.
quests.explanation: Since 'the vendor' is the subject of 'offers' (no other candidate exists), the relative pronoun must stay in every register - casual or formal. 'That' correctly introduces this subject relative clause.
options: The vendor that offers better pricing raised concerns among the team.
The vendor offers better pricing raised concerns among the team.
The vendor whom offers better pricing raised concerns among the team.
The vendor which offers pricing better raised concerns among the team.
quests.correctAnswer: The vendor that offers better pricing raised concerns among the team.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which sentence contains an error?
quests.hint: Look for a clause that needs its own subject but doesn't have one supplied anywhere.
quests.explanation: 'Needs repairs' has no other subject - 'the car' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped there.
options: The mechanic inspected the car this morning.
The car needs repairs is parked outside.
The repairs the mechanic recommended seem expensive.
The estimate she emailed arrived this afternoon.
quests.correctAnswer: The car needs repairs is parked outside.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which of these sentences has an error?
quests.hint: Look for a sentence where a connecting word has been added even though there's no second noun being described by a clause.
quests.explanation: 'I called that the mechanic yesterday' incorrectly inserts 'that' into what should be a simple sentence - there's no relative clause here at all, so 'that' doesn't belong.
options: The mechanic that I called was fully booked.
The garage I visited had a two-hour wait.
My car finally got fixed this afternoon.
I called that the mechanic yesterday.
quests.correctAnswer: I called that the mechanic yesterday.

quests.question: Which sentence below contains a mistake?
quests.hint: Three of these are correct - either they have no relative clause at all, or they correctly keep or drop the pronoun based on its role. Only one breaks the rule.
quests.explanation: 'Arrived yesterday' has no subject of its own - 'the package' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'The package that arrived yesterday was damaged.'
options: The package arrived yesterday was damaged.
The courier who delivered it apologized right away.
The refund I requested was processed quickly.
I filed a complaint about the damage.
quests.correctAnswer: The package arrived yesterday was damaged.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: The diagnosis the specialist ultimately confirmed matched her initial symptoms perfectly. What is the antecedent of the omitted clause 'the specialist ultimately confirmed'?
quests.hint: Work backward - what did the specialist actually confirm?
quests.explanation: 'The specialist confirmed' the diagnosis, so 'the diagnosis' is the antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.

quests.question: The witness statement ___ contradicted the officer's report troubled the jury.
quests.hint: Check whether 'contradicted' already has a subject elsewhere - if not, this pronoun must stay.
quests.explanation: 'Contradicted' has no other subject - 'the witness statement' must supply it, so the pronoun cannot be dropped; since a statement is a thing, 'which' is correct.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: The contract clause ___ our attorneys spent weeks negotiating finally satisfied both parties.
quests.hint: 'Our attorneys' already has a job in this clause - 'spent weeks negotiating.' What does that leave for the clause itself, and does the pronoun need to stay?
quests.explanation: 'Our attorneys' is the subject of 'spent... negotiating,' so 'the contract clause' is the object being negotiated; since a clause is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.

quests.question: The testimony of the witness the defense team thoroughly cross-examined ultimately swayed the verdict. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the defense team thoroughly cross-examined'?
quests.hint: Ask what the defense team actually cross-examined - was it the testimony itself, or the person who gave it?
quests.explanation: 'The defense team cross-examined' the witness - a person - not the testimony directly, so 'the witness' is the true antecedent of this omitted object relative clause, despite 'testimony' appearing first in the sentence.

quests.question: The recommendation from the panel of experts ___ the board is expected to approve next week has sparked internal debate.
quests.hint: 'Of experts' just tells you whose panel it is - and 'the board' already has a job in this clause. What does that leave for the recommendation, and does the pronoun need to stay?
quests.explanation: 'The board' is the subject of 'is expected to approve,' so 'the recommendation' is the object; since a recommendation is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.

quests.question: The findings of the investigation ___ ultimately confirmed every allegation.
quests.hint: 'Of the investigation' just tells you which findings - check what actually did the confirming.
quests.explanation: 'The findings' - not 'the investigation' - is what confirmed every allegation, so this is a subject relative clause; the pronoun cannot be dropped, and 'which' is correct since findings are things.

quests.question: The negotiator ___ handled the merger talks earned a substantial bonus.
quests.hint: Check whether 'handled' already has a subject elsewhere in the sentence.
quests.explanation: Nothing else performs 'handled,' so 'the negotiator' must be its subject - 'who' is correct.

quests.question: The merger ___ the negotiator handled for months finally closed.
quests.hint: 'The negotiator' already has a job in this clause - 'handled.' What does that leave for the merger, and does the pronoun need to stay?
quests.explanation: 'The negotiator' is the subject of 'handled,' so 'the merger' is the object; since a merger is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.

quests.question: The negotiator ___ reputation was built on tough deals rarely lost a client.
quests.hint: Ask what belongs to the negotiator, rather than what the negotiator is doing to someone else.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' is correct because the reputation belongs to the negotiator; this shows possession, not an action performed directly.

quests.question: The summary of the findings the lead researcher personally verified appeared in the final report. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the lead researcher personally verified'?
quests.hint: Ask what the lead researcher actually verified - the summary itself, or the underlying findings it's based on?
quests.explanation: 'The lead researcher verified' the findings, not the summary directly, so 'the findings' is the true antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.

quests.question: Which one of these sentences has a grammatical mistake?
quests.hint: Three of these sentences are correct for different reasons - either no clause is needed, or the pronoun's presence or absence correctly matches its role. Only one breaks the rule.
quests.explanation: 'Sponsored the bill' has no other subject - 'the senator' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'The senator who sponsored the bill received national attention.'
options: The proposal circulated widely before the vote.
The amendment the committee debated for hours passed narrowly.
The senator sponsored the bill received national attention.
The vote that decided the outcome was extremely close.
quests.correctAnswer: The senator sponsored the bill received national attention.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which version of this sentence would be a grammatical error no matter the register - formal or casual?
quests.hint: Unlike object relative clauses, one type of relative clause always needs its pronoun, no matter how casual the setting.
quests.explanation: 'The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families' incorrectly drops the subject relative pronoun - since 'the policy' is the subject of 'sparked' and there's no other candidate, this pronoun can never be dropped, in any register.
options: The policy that sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families.
The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families.
The families the policy affected filed a lawsuit.
The families whom the policy affected filed a lawsuit.
quests.correctAnswer: The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
